text:
The cause is of three kinds, distinguished by whether it is co‑existent, co‑existent with a condition, or a condition.  

When the effect arises together with the cause, that is a co‑existent cause—just as a thread is co‑existent with a cloth, and the cloth is co‑existent with the form of the thread.  

When the effect and the cause are united in a single sense, the cause is a co‑existent‑with‑the‑effect cause—just as the joining of a thread to a cloth is co‑existent with the thread’s form and the cloth’s form. This is a different kind of cause, called a condition (nimitta).  

When the cause is merely a condition for the effect, it is a condition cause—just as the warp (turi) is a condition for the cloth.  

Thus, among these three kinds of causes, the ordinary cause that is common to all is the cause itself.
